pezzi.35: Work that runs on its own, and lets itself be checked
pezzi.36: Flows that take repetitive work out of the way, and agents that prepare the work of judgement without deciding it. Where a signature is needed, a person stays.
pezzi.37: The mail first, then the reply
pezzi.38: First thing in the morning: which emails need an answer today, and why. The order is by urgency, not by time of arrival.
pezzi.39: Show me today’s most important emails
pezzi.42: Four emails need an answer today, ordered by urgency and not by time of arrival:
pezzi.51: Asks for an answer by Friday
pezzi.58: The other 34 are already sorted: 19 need no action, 12 filed, 3 marketing. None of them has been deleted.
pezzi.59: The agent’s job is to read and to order. It does not reply and it files nothing unless told to.
pezzi.60: Draft me a reply to Bianchi Costruzioni, with their data on record
pezzi.68: . The draft uses only what the system holds:
pezzi.78: Draft ready: it takes up the terms of June’s order, confirms the discount already applied and asks which of the three sites goes into the new quote. I have not written delivery times: the system does not hold them.
pezzi.79: AWAITING APPROVAL · nothing goes out without your yes
pezzi.80: The field that is missing stays empty and declared. That is the difference between a draft to reread and one to redo.
pezzi.81: The draft, with the customer’s data
pezzi.82: Second thing: replying. The agent reads the customer record, the orders and the terms already agreed, and writes a draft that invents nothing.
pezzi.83: The flows I keep in service
pezzi.84: Real business cases, each one tested before it is delivered. The value is not the flow: it is knowing which of the two ways is needed.
pezzi.88: It checks the data, scores it on five weighted dimensions, gives it a priority and routes it with different response times. At the end it explains why it gave that score.
pezzi.90: It checks the VAT number, the consistency between taxable amount and tax, duplicates and the gap from the historical median. It stops the ones that do not add up.
pezzi.92: It reads the official rates and gives notice only when the change goes past half a point. No pointless notifications.
pezzi.94: It classifies, assigns and routes. What it cannot classify it puts in a queue for a person, it does not guess.
pezzi.96: It sorts and files. It exists in two versions: one with the model, one without. The second is faster and always fails at the same point: it is fixed once and for all.
pezzi.98: It prepares carousels, stories and newsletters with a preview, and waits for confirmation before publishing.
pezzi.100: The question I ask first. A deterministic flow costs less, is fixed in a minute and always fails at the same point: where it is enough, I use that.
pezzi.102: When the rule can be written down
pezzi.104: When the text changes every time
pezzi.106: Knowing which of the two is needed
pezzi.108: What is repetitive and verifiable gets automated. Where judgement is needed, a person stays.
pezzi.110: An automation nobody watches becomes a silent failure. Every flow I deliver has a log, an alert when it breaks and a way to stop it: without those I do not deliver it.
